stories.body:
The Achilles heel of consumer democracies.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The Achilles heel of consumer democracies is that there is precious little constituency for the future in the present. All the feedback signals — in politics, culture and the market — are geared to short-term gratification. In each case, the incentives of the system deliver what the most influential demographic wants, and when they want it, which is now.

From fast fashion to electoral contests to quarterly earnings reports, the system is responsive to the pursuit of happiness defined by the near horizon.

The consequence of this, which Harvard sociologist Daniel Bell argued more than half a century ago in his book, “The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism,” is that the present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society. The recent Noema essay by Simon Curtis and Ian Klaus titled “Americans Are Losing The Long Game” is excellent on this point.

While state-guided dirigiste policies that champion and support strategic industries deemed critical for the future are roundly frowned upon in market economies, the opposite rigidity of the short-term consumerist mentality is less appreciated as a critical failure of good governance. Yet, unless societies prepare for, subsidize and invest in the kind of future they want, they will never get there.

“The present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society.”

China’s Market-State Modality

Of all the major powers, post-Mao China stands out in taking control of its future without sacrificing the present. Over recent decades, it has both lifted hundreds of millions into general prosperity while, at the same time, swiftly conquering the key industries of a sustainable future, from green technology to artificial intelligence.

One has to admit that the Middle Kingdom’s mix of a long-term planning framework checked by robust market signals and bolstered by strategically deployed subsidies has worked. Indeed, it has worked too well: Its overproduction is spilling out and flooding world markets, threatening to displace domestic jobs and industry elsewhere.

China has not arrived at this point overnight. It has been a long time coming. In 1987, the ideology chief of the Communist Party politburo at the time, Hu Qili, told me in Beijing: “The market is not a feature unique to capitalism. Capitalism does not have the patent right over the market economy. What we are trying to create is a new and unprecedented modality where planning is combined with the commodity economy, where the state regulates the market, and the market guides the enterprises.”

The overall economy is steered by a one-party political system designed to reach consensus over long-term goals that have the decisive thrust to be carried out over many years without a break in continuity. Once set, the policy path is followed with relative discipline by a leadership and administration that, while not based on popular appeal to an electorate, is systemically accountable for realizing its set objectives.

When a key strategic goal is ordained by the Party, the state fosters a “whole dragon” approach in which start-up subsidies, sourcing, supply chains and production capacity are vertically aligned, making it one of the most powerful production ensembles in economic history.

Flaws Linked To Strength

The chief flaw of China’s system, of course, is closely linked to its strength. To keep the consensus from fraying, it overcompensates on the side of repressive order and control of freedom. It is the opposite of the open societies of the West, where the flaw lies within the strength of diverse participation and electoral competition: a growing inability to forge a consensus on long-term goals out of the cacophony of voices, the welter of contending interests and the immediate wash of fickle public opinion.

When all-out competitive partisanship destroys consensus among the body politic, the democratic transfer of power can mean a complete rupture of policies endorsed by most voters only four years earlier. Sticking to the course for the time it takes to reach fruition is not a reliable feature of this system.

The extreme edge of this stark difference can be seen in the contrasting behavior of the current leadership in the U.S. and China. America’s leader relishes dominating the memes of the moment, battling his way through every 24-hour news cycle by firing off social media barrages at sundry foes. China’s near-dictatorial leader has used his amassed clout to chart out a roadmap for the next half century.

China’s Long March To Owning Green Technologies

Meeting in Mexico in 2012, the G-20 decided for the first time to put climate change on the agenda. In those days, the Berggruen Institute’s 21 st Century Council, a group of former heads of state and government, tech leaders and Nobel laureates, would meet with the chair of the G-20 each year to advise on its agenda. Read Noema in print.

That year’s chair, then Mexican president Felipe Calderón, invited the council for lunch in the garden of Los Pinos, the presidential palace, to discuss the upcoming meeting. When the topic turned to climate, Wu Jianmin, a top Chinese diplomat and executive director of the China Institute for Innovation and Development Strategy, related that a top priority of the then incoming Party leadership of Xi Jinping would be “ecological civilization.”

All those 14 years ago, he confidently laid out a trajectory of China’s decisive shift to electric vehicles and plans for massive R&D investment in battery storage for wind and solar as well as EVs. Everyone listened respectfully, but doubtfully, because China was then not even in the auto race.

In 2012, China already dominated solar panels, but the Chevy Volt was the world’s most produced EV. No nation commanded battery production, which then was only nascently entering global competition.

Wu’s confidence in China’s capacity to deliver was well-founded. Today, nearly 70% of all new car sales in China are EVs, and half of all sales globally are Chinese-made electric vehicles. China produces around 80% of the world’s batteries and holds 70% of global battery patents. Its hosts half of the entire world’s large-scale battery storage capacity, primarily to store solar and wind power for the grid when the sun isn’t shining or the wind blowing.

As part of its whole-dragon approach, China also built out the widely distributed infrastructure of rapid charging stations across the country necessary to boost EV use. It launched a strategic push to link battery storage to the grid, requiring developers to build or commission large-scale storage capacity as a condition for approval of new wind or solar installations.

China’s export of its technology has enabled the advance of large-scale batteries for integration into power grids in many countries. Some 70% of EV batteries worldwide are from China.

California has the most installed large battery storage facilities outside of China. Its capacity has grown from a mere 700 megawatts in 2019 to 21,000 MW in 2026. By 2045, the state aims to reach 52,000 MW capacity to support a 100% clean energy grid. For the entire month of May 2026, 51% of California’s total energy demand came from solar power. Blackouts during the intense heatwaves of recent years have been avoided because the grid was linked to off-hour battery storage from renewable energy.

Though often assembled in California, 90% of the cells and core components of the large-scale batteries the state has installed come from China.

Quotas And Dumping

From the standpoint of the race against time on climate, the widest possible dispersion of China’s green technology is a net plus for the planet. Yet, as in other realms of trade competition, its cheaper product and overproduction portends a vulnerable dependence on a political system which the West considers a strategic adversary.

To the extent domestic industries exist, China’s prowess threatens to run them out of business. Since green technology is critical to our future, the most sensible approach would not be to prohibit Chinese imports, but set a reasonable quota beyond which tariffs would kick in. That would both limit the damage while allowing competition from abroad to spark the scale-up of domestic industry.

Free-market ideologues aside, subsidies are not the end of the world when a livable biosphere is at stake. After all, up until the Trump administration, the U.S. did manage for a time to escape the pull of consumer immediacy. For years, it subsidized the purchase of EVs with tax rebates. And California has shown how regulation creates, not destroys, markets. Elon Musk’s Tesla empire would never have emerged if it were not for the state’s fuel efficiency and clean energy standards, which created the market for his technology.

“Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China?”

Is It Impolitic To Learn From China?

Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China? This is not, of course, to imply in any way that the West turn toward autocracy or authoritarianism. It is only to warn that unless democracies can look beyond the short-term horizon and find ways to reach a governing consensus that sticks, they will be left in the dust of the oncoming future.

To turn an old Chinese saying toward ourselves: “The stones from hills yonder can polish jade at home.”

stories.title: Judge rejects Trump’s wild claim EPA can dismiss data center pollution lawsuits
stories.summary: Trump’s EPA can't unilaterally dismiss SpaceXAI pollution lawsuit, court rules.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump’s EPA can’t unilaterally dismiss SpaceXAI pollution lawsuit, court rules.

Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI is stuck facing a lawsuit over alleged data center pollution after Donald Trump failed to convince a judge that his Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has complete control over all Clean Air Act lawsuits and can dismiss any suit at whim.

Soon after unpermitted gas turbines were discovered powering Musk’s giant Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, the NAACP sued . Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI (which, following a merger , is known now as SpaceXAI) to use the best available pollution control technology when operating the turbines and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. Without such remedies, the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby, the NAACP argued.

To block the lawsuit, Trump tried to intervene, arguing that the EPA had the power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. According to Trump, it would supposedly “not serve the public interest” if citizens were allowed to seek massive civil penalties to punish polluting AI firms that were trying to get data centers operational as fast as possible to support Trump’s AI Action Plan .

But Trump’s efforts to spare Musk’s firm were halted by a federal judge Tuesday, who ruled that “nothing” in the Clean Air Act (CAA) allows the EPA Administrator to “unilaterally dismiss a citizen suit.”

Such a power grab would seemingly give Trump authority to block any lawsuits alleging data center pollution, US District Judge Debra Brown’s order suggested. Even further, she observed that Trump could have used the authority to defend any interests against CAA lawsuits, not just the AI industry’s.

The NAACP had argued that the CAA’s text is focused “on ensuring air pollution standards are met and people are protected.” It urged the court to recognize that there is “no way to read” a provision granting citizens a right to sue as Trump has. That would “suggest that Congress, having gone out of its way to preserve people’s ability to sue to stop unlawful pollution when the government has not, also implicitly authorized the government to dismiss those very suits at its whim because it would prefer that the unlawful pollution continue,” the NAACP successfully argued.

In a press release, Laura Thoms—an enforcement director for an environmental group called Earthjustice that has partnered with the NAACP to support the lawsuit—accused Trump of seeking “unilateral and unreviewable veto power over citizen suits.”

“The Trump Administration has gone out of its way to shield Elon Musk’s company, [SpaceXAI], from liability and to deny local communities their right to protect themselves against illegal pollution,” Thoms said.

Thoms’ group is monitoring data center fights nationwide, not just SpaceXAI’s Colossus fight. However, Musk’s company’s battle was the first to expose the AI industry’s increasingly common practice of using unpermitted gas turbines to keep data center goals on target. So, Brown’s ruling is likely viewed as a big win for Americans worried Trump might make it impossible to stop the AI industry from polluting communities at a critical moment when data center demand for gas turbines is exploding .

Praising the court for “denying the US’s unprecedented and alarming argument,” Thoms vowed to “continue the fight to hold xAI accountable for the illegal air pollution it has been pumping out around the clock.”

Trump’s deeply flawed argument

Brown slammed the Trump EPA’s reading of the CAA as an “extraordinary position” with no grounding in federal law.

Trump tried to warp a single exception that lets the EPA dismiss a CAA lawsuit when it is either suing to require CAA enforcement or otherwise acting to require compliance.

Neither situation applies in this case, where the Trump administration has made it clear that it has no intention to sue SpaceXAI over the alleged violations. The federal government’s decision to ignore the problem is partly why the citizen lawsuit is necessary, the NAACP argued.

In that scenario where Trump could have dismissed the NAACP’s lawsuit, courts recognize that a citizen lawsuit could clash with government efforts to enforce the CAA or reach agreements with violators. But in the SpaceXAI lawsuit, Trump argued that the government’s right to intervene, which is sometimes used to dismiss lawsuits, was enough to shut down this lawsuit, regardless of the other facts.

Brown pointed out that it made no sense to argue that citizens can’t raise CAA lawsuits that the EPA opposes when the CAA also grants a right to sue the EPA administrator for failing to enforce the CAA.

“Evidently, Congress contemplated that citizen suits may not always align with the EPA’s judgment,” Brown wrote.

Congress even contemplated granting powers close to the authority Trump’s EPA tried to assert in this case, Brown said in a footnote. In 1990, Congress considered amending the CAA so that the EPA could substitute itself and take control of citizen suits over alleged violations. Had that happened, Trump may have been able to step in and drop the lawsuit. However, Congress did not adopt that amendment back in 1990, and Brown suggested that the mere consideration of the amendment favored the NAACP’s reading of the CAA.

“At most, the proposed amendment is evidence that at least some members of the 1990 Congress believed that the citizen suit provision as written does not allow the Administrator to intervene and subsequently terminate a citizen plaintiff’s claim,” Brown wrote.

Judge denies EPA veto power

Brown also acknowledged that the NAACP’s argument that every case Trump tried to use to seize power to veto the lawsuit “arose in a context where a government acted to require abatement of unlawful pollution, not one where the government acted to shield the polluter from liability.”

Ultimately, she agreed that “because the Administrator has not taken any action to enforce the Clean Air Act here, these cases do not support the United States’ position.”

Trump seemed particularly upset that SpaceXAI may face large fines. He argued that “punishing unlawful conduct through civil penalties payable to the Treasury on behalf of the United States is ‘a quintessentially executive power.’” As Trump explained, because the CAA is too vague on this point, “the canon of constitutional avoidance” applies, and courts must err on the side of his administration. Simply dismissing the lawsuit would avoid a constitutional clash, Trump argued.

But once again, Brown disagreed.

The US “fails to identify any ambiguity in the statute’s text to which the Court could and should apply the canon of constitutional avoidance,” Brown wrote. Rejecting Trump’s constitutional “doubts,” she concluded that “constitutional avoidance does not allow the Court to invent a right that does not exist in the statute.”

“That the Clean Air Act’s citizen suit provision allows private parties to enforce the Clean Air Act through civil litigation, therefore, does not make citizen suits an impermissible exercise of the President’s executive power,” Brown wrote. And “it does not follow that all suits seeking civil penalties require the exercise of nondelegable executive power.”

Had Trump succeeded, Americans who are increasingly opposing data centers nationwide may have been widely blocked from seeking fines when pollution can be proven.

Brown said the CAA cannot be interpreted that way, though, since “it can scarcely be doubted that, for a plaintiff who is injured or faces the threat of future injury due to illegal conduct ongoing at the time of suit, a sanction that effectively abates that conduct and prevents its recurrence provides a form of redress. Civil penalties can fit that description.” Critically, “to the extent that they encourage defendants to discontinue current violations and deter them from committing future ones, they afford redress to citizen plaintiffs who are injured or threatened with injury as a consequence of ongoing unlawful conduct,” Brown wrote.

Trump never explained intervention

When Trump took his first stab at blocking the lawsuit this summer, he didn’t cite EPA authority, just his own. He later amended his motion to specify that he was intervening on behalf of the EPA after the NAACP, and the court immediately pointed out fatal flaws in his arguments.

Since then, Brown’s order suggests that Trump’s efforts to kill Musk’s lawsuit stayed messy.

As a prime example, Trump goofed up by prematurely filing his appeal after the district court merely acknowledged at a hearing that it intended to dismiss the government’s motion to intervene to drop the suit. Without waiting for the actual opinion to drop, the US quickly went to an appeals court to reverse an order that did not exist yet, Brown said.

On the day that Brown at last issued her order, it did not say what Trump expected it to say. Parsing the actual order, the appeals court agreed that Trump had filed his appeal prematurely and denied Trump’s request to stay the district court’s litigation.

The appeals court denial came largely because Trump’s appeal was premised on Brown denying the government’s motion to intervene, which she did not. Although Brown denied Trump’s request to dismiss the lawsuit, she is still allowing the government to intervene on other grounds to support SpaceXAI, if that’s its intent.

That point remains somewhat unclear, as Brown noted that the government, in its rush to intervene, never said why it’s intervening—apart from bluntly demanding the suit be dropped. She gave the government until October 23 to either explain its position or stay out of the litigation.

stories.title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
stories.summary: The prime minister provided little detail, and there are questions over shifting the fees onto unit costs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 October 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.

These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.

Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.

But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill.

During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".

He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".

No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate , external , so people pay for what they use.

This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.

For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.

Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.

Higher cost of electricity standing charges

Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas.

When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills.

Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure.

The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households.

Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, but Citizens Advice has warned , external about the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers.

Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised.

But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices."

Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy prices forecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January .

In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament".

Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries.

stories.title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
stories.summary: The UK government says the field, which is opposed by environmental campaigners, could be producing gas by the end of this month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal on Wednesday

Published 21 October 2026

The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.

She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".

"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.

The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank

The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.

She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences.

"We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.

The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".

He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".

Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.

The Jackdaw platform is located east of Aberdeen

Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.

"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.

He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."

Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.

This video can not be played

Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial?

But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning

Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.

The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.

Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.

But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully .

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.

The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.

BBC News visited the Jackdaw platform this summer

When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.

However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined , external .

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.

UK government approves drilling in Jackdaw gas field with production to start this month

Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain Published 19 hours ago

What is happening with the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields? Published 20 hours ago

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

stories.title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
stories.summary: Education Secretary Lucy Powell has stressed the importance of reminding new generations of the horrors of the Holocaust.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 October 2026

Education Secretary Lucy Powell says the government will "update and strengthen" Holocaust education within schools after a major review highlighted the "shocking scale" of antisemitism in British society.

Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it.

It means anti-Jewish hatred will be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying.

The government has accepted all of the 27 recommendations made in the government-commissioned review including dedicated training for teachers and more consistent recording of incidents.

Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says Published 1 day ago

The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday.

Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent".

She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges.

"I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next – that is the job of education – to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world."

Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have.

The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.

Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics.

The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.

Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.

The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.

It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters .

The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."

Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said.

"We think about it a lot."

In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism".

They said: "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition."

Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day".

"Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged."

"One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust."

The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition.

It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza".

The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised".

Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.

It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year.

stories.title: Jailed former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson being investigated over alleged rape inside Parliament
stories.summary: While not naming the disgraced former MP, the Metropolitan Police has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Donaldson arriving at Newry Crown Court for a previous court appearance in June

Published 21 October 2026

Jailed former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated by London police about an alleged rape of a woman inside the Houses of Parliament, the BBC can reveal.

The disgraced former MP has been accused of raping the woman in Parliament in 2016, at the very heart of the political establishment.

Last week Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions.

It is understood the woman has been interviewed by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers.

The PSNI has now shared her claims with the Metropolitan Police, as the alleged incident happened in London.

While not naming the former DUP leader, the Met has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.

It said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report referred to us by the Police Service of Northern Ireland relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.

"The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers.

"The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."

In July, the Belfast Telegraph first reported that a woman from Northern Ireland alleged she had been sexually assaulted by Donaldson in the DUP offices at Parliament in 2016.

She claimed that he attempted to get her to drink vodka shots in his office, before trying to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt.

On Saturday, the newspaper further reported that the Met was set to investigate and interview Donaldson about these accusations.

But in response to BBC questions it has now emerged the same woman has also alleged Donaldson raped her.

Concerns about the ex-DUP MP's behaviour in London were raised in a BBC NI Spotlight film , earlier this year.

A former senior PSNI detective told the programme he had seen Donaldson drunk in the Houses of Parliament.

Two other former senior PSNI detectives also reported seeing him going into a gay sauna not far from Parliament in 2006, the same year in which Donaldson described homosexuality as "sinful".

stories.title: Tory MP questions government advisor's position after wife's Palestine Action post
stories.summary: A Downing Street spokeswoman tells the BBC Sarah Helm "does not represent the government in any capacity".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Alicia Kearns has written to the prime minister

Published 20 October 2026

Conservative MP Alicia Kearns has raised concerns over whether Jonathan Powell, the national security adviser, can remain in his post following his wife's references to Palestine Action on social media.

The shadow home affairs minister has written to the PM asking if Powell's position is still tenable, despite the Metropolitan Police concluding no action was necessary over his wife, Sarah Helm's, comments.

A No 10 spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."

Posting on X last week, Helm wrote: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action," responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney.

The Normal People writer announced last week that her books will not be supplied to UK booksellers after she announced she would use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

The Met investigation into Helm's post found "it did not meet the criminal threshold" and the matter was dropped on Saturday.

But Kearns has written to Andy Burnham about the handling of sensitive national security information, asking whether the government has investigated the posts and whether he retains full confidence in his adviser.

She told the BBC: "We cannot have the NSA's [national security adviser's] wife tweeting about what decisions her husband has or hasn't made."

On Monday, Helm responded to a question on X about whether her husband had been involved in the decision to ban Palestine Action with the reply "nope".

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation last year, making it a a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years imprisonment to belong to or support the group.

An appeal against the proscription of Palestine Action is due to be heard by the Supreme Court next month , external , in a battle that has now gone on for more than year.

The Labour Against Antisemitism group also wrote to the prime minister, calling for Powell to either resign or be sacked.

The organisation pointed to Helm's social media posts, including one from 2018 when she wrote: "Palestinians have never had their voice heard in British corridors of power. They have no equivalent of the Jewish lobby here.

"No access to ministers, still less prime ministers."

The letter said Helm discussed her husband's work publicly and cited a 2016 article she wrote for the Guardian , external in which she revealed details of a conversation she had overheard between George Bush and Tony Blair, when her husband had been the No 10 chief of staff.

The group said Helm would have been included in the vetting process when Powell took on the NSA role.

"Either Jonathan Powell lacks full clearance, vetting missed this, or saw it. Each is indefensible," the letter said.

stories.title: Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
stories.summary: The economic figures released on Wednesday show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his Budget.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 October 2026

The chancellor was on an early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped.

From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms.

The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures.

The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months.

Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase.

These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week.

On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.

The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs.

While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased.

From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year.

The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month.

The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output.

Cost of living trade off

The latest inflation figure also applies as the uprating to tens of billions in welfare payments next April.

By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.

The figure also confirms that the Triple Lock will see the State Pension increase by 3.9% next April.

There is one form of relief here - food price inflation remains largely unaffected by the energy shock.

While higher inflation at a time of frozen tax thresholds will raise more tax in cash terms, it will also increase the cost of public services, including likely union pay demands.

All the while, UK borrowing costs have risen alongside most of the advanced world as the US-Israel war against Iran has intensified.

The Jackdaw gas field decision is seen as the start of a run of "pro growth" pre-Budget announcements.

It sends a directional message, but will not fundamentally change the trade off between cost of living breathing space, and delivering a Budget that convinces the markets and investors.

The fact the borrowing costs gap has narrowed a bit with other G7 nations, and the IMF praised pencilled-in plans to shrink borrowing, provided a platform for the chancellor's Budget.

The latest economic numbers amply illustrate the challenge of actually delivering them.

stories.title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
stories.summary: Inflation accelerated to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 October 2026

UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week.

The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running £6bn above official forecasts.

Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules.

Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September. It is the highest inflation has been since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies.

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.

Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.

ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.

As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.

September's inflation figure is also important because it suggests how benefits will increase next April.

It means the state pension will most likely rise by 3.9%, in line with average wage rises from May to July, due to the triple lock.

The inflation figure for September also dictates how other benefits will rise in April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.

With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide."

He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field .

The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space".

But the inflation figure came as the ONS said the government borrowed £24.5bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs.

The overshoot means, cumulatively, the government has borrowed £6bn more this year than the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which scores government spending plans, had forecast.

Despite overall debt topping £3tn for the first time, debt as a proportion of the UK's economic output - the measure used by the government to judge whether it is in line with its fiscal rules - fell.

Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge Published 18 hours ago

The Conservatives said higher inflation and borrowing showed Labour had "lost control of the economy".

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith called for Healey to use his Budget to "tackle the deficit, and reduce the red tape and net zero costs that are driving up the cost of living for families".

He added that the Conservatives would cut taxes, the costs of benefits and "wasteful" spending to "make our country prosperous again".

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the borrowing figures "painted a dismal picture" ahead of Healey's Budget. She said the amount borrowed in September was higher than analyst expectations as well as spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)'s forecast.

"This reinforces our view that the Chancellor will deliver a cautious Budget on 28 October that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year," she said.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
stories.summary: Jackdaw and Rosebank are case studies in the slow motion awkwardness the UK has over energy.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 October 2026

The decision to grant approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea and the further delay in a decision about the Rosebank oil field, also in the North Sea, are case studies in the slow-motion awkwardness the UK has collectively had, over years, about energy.

At the heart of that awkwardness, these questions: where should our energy come from, and with what costs and consequences, for the customer and for the environment?

Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has talked about a desire to be "pragmatic" about the North Sea as he puts it, which is why this decision about Jackdaw isn't a surprise.

In fact it felt near inevitable after President Trump blurted out – after his first phone call with Burnham in the summer – that the prime minister had told him he would "open up the North Sea".

Burnham acknowledged the two leaders had discussed the issue, arguing: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that."

What we now know is the government is approving drilling of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

A decision on Rosebank, an oil field about 80 miles north east of Shetland, is expected to take a bit longer.

UK government approves Jackdaw gas field and says production will start this month

The city caught in the middle of the big energy shift debate Published 30 April

What is happening with the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields? Published 20 hours ago

The timeline of back and forth about both projects is worth revisiting. Jackdaw was first approved four years ago, Rosebank three years ago.

But after a legal challenge by environmental campaigners, it was ruled that consent had been granted unlawfully and there needed to be a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact.

And then, of course – there is politics, international and domestic, between parties and within parties.

Debate about energy security and spiralling prices, given the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the environmental impact, carbon emissions and the message new drilling sends to the wider world.

But others point to the extra carbon emissions when energy is imported, the tax revenues generated from domestic energy and the social and economic consequences of the British oil and gas sector deindustrialising too quickly and, in particular, the impact on cities such as Aberdeen.

Then, for the government, there are the promises the Labour Party made when it was seeking your support at the general election in 2024.

Page 52 of Labour's manifesto reads like a rhetorical twister – a paragraph of promises seeking to stretch in multiple directions at the same time, trying to keep a breadth of people happy simultaneously, or perhaps not annoy too many people too much.

"Labour will not revoke existing licences and we will partner with business and workers to manage our existing fields for the entirety of their lifespan. Crucially, oil and gas production in the North Sea will be with us for decades to come, and the North Sea will be managed in a way that does not jeopardise jobs," it reads.

"And our offshore workers will lead the world in the industries of the future. We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis," it adds.

Crucially, the Jackdaw and Rosebank licences had already been issued, leaving political wriggle room on these two outstanding and high profile decisions the Labour government inherited on taking office.

But the multiple trade-offs, of course, remain very real, including for some of the key individuals involved.

Miatta Fahnbulleh took over from Ed Miliband as energy secretary earlier this yer

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who used to be the energy secretary, has long been vocal about what he sees as the need to move away from fossil fuels.

His successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who has announced this decision, previously wrote , external that "to have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can't have any new oil or gas fields," adding "it's irresponsible and short sighted to be funding new fossil fuels when we need to get to Net Zero fast."

Fahnbulleh has today told BBC Radio Scotland gas from Jackdaw will be "in our homes and businesses this month" but acknowledged that it "won't lower our energy bills this winter".

Instead, she is grounding her argument for approving this in energy security and saying the tax revenue generated will go into an "Energy Wealth Fund" to pay for "low carbon and renewable projects".

Rosebank, she added, was a "different proposition" as its oil would be exported, but she will "look at it".

Politically, the decision on Jackdaw is considerably easier for the government than the decision on Rosebank.

Broadly speaking, most Labour MPs are comfortable with endorsing Jackdaw. It is also a project backed by the Conservatives and Reform (who argue a decision should have been taken much sooner) and the Scottish National Party and the Liberal Democrats. The Green Party of England and Wales are opposed.

On Rosebank, the argument is much more contentious within the Labour Party. Some, who can see the rationale for Jackdaw cannot see it for Rosebank. Bluntly, it is a much more difficult decision, as Fahnbulleh has acknowledged.

What we can expect in the coming hours and days - as it has started already - is a resumption of all the arguments these projects have already provoked, with some saying approval should have happened ages ago, alongside plenty more.

And others arguing the announcement is utterly irresponsible.

stories.title: What is happening to UK prices?
stories.summary: UK inflation rose in September, pushed up by higher petrol and diesel prices.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 January 2011

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target.

The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.

Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months.

What is inflation?

Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%.

How is the UK's inflation rate measured and what does it mean for UK interest rates?

The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026 , while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed.

The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation.

The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) , external , and the latest figure is published every month.

The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%.

Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises.

But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy.

For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals.

Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment.

What is happening to UK inflation?

Although CPI inflation of 3.5% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

That was the highest rate for 40 years.

While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly.

The higher figure for September was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 29.8% compared to September last year.

Food price inflation remained at 1.3%.

But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran.

How do energy prices affect UK inflation?

Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine.

Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026.

But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario.

When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July .

As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the 4% increase in household energy bills from 1 October when the latest Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher.

As part of his pledge to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living, Prime Minister Andy Burnham scrapped VAT on household electricity bills in October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation.

Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs.

Core CPI was 2.8% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to August.

Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 October

What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 28 September

What does an Andy Burnham-led government mean for your money? Published 22 July

What is happening to UK interest rates and will they fall again?

The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023.

In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario.

At its September meeting , Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.

Are wages keeping up with inflation?

The Bank also looks closely at what is happening to wages and unemployment.

The latest official figures show that regular pay in the UK grew ahead of inflation in the three months to August.

Average annual growth in pay, excluding bonuses, during the three-month period was 3.7%.

After taking inflation into account, it means regular pay grew by 0.8% between June and August.

The 20-somethings juggling three jobs to make ends meet Published 21 April

What needs to change to get more people working? Published 5 November 2025

What is happening to inflation and interest rates in Europe and the US?

The US and eurozone countries have also been trying to limit price increases, but also face challenges with inflation.

The inflation rate for countries using the euro was 3.8% in September, according to EU data , external - up from 3.2% in August.

The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in recent months to 2.5%.

US inflation was in 3.7% in September , up from 3.4% in August, with prices there also affected by higher fuel costs.

The Federal Reserve cited "too high" inflation when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%.

The move came despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong

D oes Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.

Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal . European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.

The Wall Street Journal laid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite most analysts saying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ‌energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. More Republicans should find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from the White House . Heated denials from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , are no substitute for answers.

A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “ strategically and culturally vital ”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments must prepare to meet that challenge.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo the Three Emperors’ League that brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in 1881 , the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men.

stories.summary: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for more than 50 years , and in the U.S. since 1998 ), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime. In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance. Since 2012 , EFF has worked with others to expose the severe digital rights harms of ALPR systems. For example, we’ve recently documented how these camera networks allow law enforcement to search for immigrants , track peaceful protesters , target Romani communities , and track women seeking reproductive healthcare . Police also routinely use ALPRs for low-level matters like enforcing school residency requirements or investigating noise complaints . Many officers also use ALPR databases to stalk past romantic partners . Recent EFF analysis revealed officers using the system without legitimate justification—logging search reasons like "LOL" and "LMAO." Understandably, the public backlash to police ALPR technology is accelerating, and state lawmakers across the country are taking action. New Hampshire enacted the nation’s first state law on ALPR use in 2007, but technological advances and misconduct have driven even more recent legislative action. "Parents don’t need to be technology experts to help their children navigate the digital world safely” said EFF Public Interest Technology Director Babette Ngene. “At EFF, we believe in empowering families with the knowledge and confidence to make informed decisions about their digital lives. It’s about meeting families where they are and giving parents the guidance they need to have meaningful conversations with their children about digital safety, based on what works best for their families.” EFF launches this crucial resource as state and local governments consider enacting well-meaning but ill-advised laws that cut young people off from essential information and experiences, particularly harming vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. Such laws also entail age gating, which compromises the privacy of all internet users and stifles young users’ ability to learn, grow, and express themselves. “Deciding how to help your young people use the internet—including engaging with video games, social media, web search, and everything else—is a complicated topic that touches on many different skillsets and ideas,” said EFF Senior Security and Privacy Activist Thorin Klosowski. “But ultimately it's up to families – not governments – to decide when and how to engage with these sorts of questions.” Each young person has unique needs, and, just like their wardrobe, that changes as they age. stories.title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful
stories.summary: In a victory for data privacy, a federal court in New York definitively ruled that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) violated the law when it disclosed millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. In a summary judgment ruling issued on October 20, 2026, the court found that OPM violated two provisions of the Privacy Act—one restricting disclosure of personal records between agencies and another requiring agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of records. Since the case was filed, many DOGE agents have left the government and OPM has rescinded their database access. However, OPM should still clean up the cybersecurity mess it created. The court will decide the remedy at a later date. "By virtue of the Court’s summary judgment ruling, OPM’s decision to grant DOGE Agents broad access to its systems of recordings containing [personally identifiable information (PII)] has been held unlawful," Judge Denise Cote wrote. "The record also provides no support for a finding that it was the pursuit of a modernization agenda that prompted OPM to grant sweeping and expedited access to a score of DOGE Agents to its systems of records containing PII," she added. OPM maintains databases of highly sensitive personal information about tens of millions of federal employees, retirees, and job applicants. Starting in January 2025, OPM disclosed data to the U.S. DOGE Service, initially led by Elon Musk. This disclosure violates the federal Privacy Act of 1974, a watershed anti-surveillance statute that prevents the federal government from abusing our personal information. EFF sued OPM and DOGE because this data disclosure violates the Privacy Act. We represent unions of federal employees – the American Federation of Government Employees and the Association of Administrative Law Judges – and individual employees. We seek injunctive and declaratory relief. We filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Our co-counsel are Lex Lumina LLP , State Democracy Defenders Fund , and The Chandra Law Firm LLC . stories.title: EFF to Brazil’s ANPD: Data Privacy and Free Expression Must Underpin Platform Regulations
stories.summary: The Brazilian National Data Protection Agency (ANPD) plays a pivotal role in the regulation of digital platforms according to new legislation approved in Brazil. Throughout this year, EFF has presented comments, filed submissions, and met with the agency to emphasize crucial guardrails that the enforcement of new regulations should ensure. ANPD is responsible for detailing and applying obligations set in Law n. 15.211/2025, which established rules for the protection of children and adolescents in the digital space. While some provisions establish important privacy safeguards, like prohibiting advertising based on profiling of underage users, the law created mandatory age assurance mechanisms for accessing digital products and services. We have raised alarms on the privacy and free expression issues around age-gating the internet. Age verification technology is often inaccurate and privacy-invasive . Examples also show how it’s prone to enforcement overreach, resulting in sites blocked beyond legal requirements. In the UK, providers disproportionately restricted several counseling, support and mental health sites under the Online Safety Act. Current age assurance methods risk wrongly walling off adults with no valid IDs , facial differences , physical disabilities , among others. We highlighted these concerns in our comments and submissions underscoring that ANPD should avoid a blanket approach to age assurance obligations. Following the legislation, restrictions should apply only to products and services that are inadequate or prohibited to children and adolescents according to categories already set in regulation, with robust protections against subjective and overbroad interpretations. Guarantees such as access to information, freedom to participate in society and meaningful access to technologies also compound what constitutes the best interests of the child. Moreover, we stressed that zero knowledge proofs alone fail to ensure strong user privacy, including safeguards that the law itself sought to secure. Our submission explains why other requirements, such as unlinkability, selective disclosure, batch issuance and processing on device, are crucial for achieving greater levels of protection and mitigating privacy harms. Minimum information being shared to the verifier and no “phoning home” to the issuer of a user’s accepted credentials are conditions…

stories.title: Require Police to Get a Warrant to Search ALPR Data
stories.summary: This post was co-written by Andi Cao , an EFF legal intern. Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives. Cities should not buy them , and cities that already have them should shut them down. Where these systems still operate, courts and state legislatures must reduce their harms by (among other things) requiring police to get a warrant before searching stored ALPR data. A warrant requirement would not make mass surveillance acceptable, but it would require police to justify a search to a judge before accessing records of people’s movements. Without this independent judicial check on police power, officers have been searching this data for improper reasons (many exposed by EFF) that violate our fundamental rights. A warrant requires a judge to find probable cause and specificity—many warrantless police searches of ALPR data lack both. Officers have searched this data to profile Romani people, monitor protesters, investigate an abortion, find immigrants for deportation, track a man who complained about a deputy, stalk romantic partners, and even for no stated reason beyond “LMAO.” A warrant requirement would force law enforcement to justify these searches before accessing sensitive location records, not leave the people they target to discover and challenge the abuse after the harm is done. What a Warrant Requires Warrants are a check on police power. Before officers can search a person or their property, the Fourth Amendment requires them to convince a neutral judge, under oath, that probable cause exists, meaning a fair probability the search will turn up evidence of a crime. The warrant must also describe with particularity what will be searched, so police cannot go on a fishing expedition. Critically, the officer who wants to search is not the person who decides whether the search is justified. That is why warrants are required for so many kinds of police surveillance. For example, police generally need a warrant to wiretap phone calls , to search the contents of a cell phone , and to obtain historical cell phone location records . stories.title: Everyone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?
stories.summary: In a few days the busiest shopping street in Europe will be closed to traffic. The hope is that an unloved and polluted thoroughfare will turn into somewhere that people actually want to spend time In February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in. This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe , attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling. Continue reading...
